Introduction

The GUIDARS team (David Cejas, Tomás Arancibia, and Tomás Lopreite) worked on the “Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map” challenge for NASA Space Apps 2026. We created a 3D route planner for future astronauts on the surface of Mars, built using real data from NASA missions.

The tool plans an expedition for two astronauts on the actual terrain. The two depart from the habitat, located in an area selected for landing by our suitability analysis. They travel together in a pressurized rover (PMR) and make stops chosen from among Curiosity’s drill sites and waypoints. At each stop, one astronaut walks to the scientific site while the other remains in the PMR, which serves as a mobile shelter and support vehicle. On foot, they drill deeper holes than Curiosity and install instruments such as magnetometers and seismometers. The expedition ends near Curiosity’s current location, where they collect samples, and then return to the habitat. At each stage, the tool displays the safest route for the vehicle and the astronaut, the slope, the cumulative radiation dose, the time to the shelter, and the scientific purpose of the stop.

We are working in Gale Crater, where the Curiosity rover has been exploring for more than 14 years. It is the location on Mars with the most ground-based data. We combine the USGS elevation model, HiRISE images, CRISM mineralogy, RAD radiation data, REMS weather data, Curiosity’s actual trajectory with its 49 drill holes, and extensive information from instruments and orbiters. The rest of the planet appears only as general context, the detailed analysis focuses on Gale.

 

 

 

 

 

Development

Starting point

Astronauts will need to know which routes they can safely take, how much radiation they will receive along the way, and how far they are from shelter at every moment. NASA’s Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge asks for exactly that: an interface that brings together data from several missions to guide an astronaut on the surface, with routes that avoid obstacles and respect limits such as radiation and suit mobility.

What changes when the same terrain is crossed by a person instead of a rover? A rover is limited by slope, sand and power, and can take weeks to cover a few kilometres. An astronaut can cover the same ground in a single outing, but is limited by suit mobility, time away from shelter and radiation dose. Comparing both on the same real terrain shows what a human crew gains and what new risks it has to manage.

To answer it, we chose Gale Crater. Curiosity has been exploring it since 2012, which makes it the most thoroughly ground-truthed place on Mars: its elevation, minerals, radiation and weather have been measured on the ground or mapped from orbit at high resolution. Our goal was to turn that knowledge into decisions for a crew, planning a human expedition that follows Curiosity’s path and builds on what it discovered, without disturbing the historic traverse.

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

Data

Our project is built entirely on public data from NASA missions and their partners, mainly ESA and USGS. We organized it in four groups: orbital data that describe the terrain, measurements taken on the ground by Curiosity, engineering references for astronauts and vehicles, and the values we calculated or assumed ourselves. Every value in the tool carries its source, and the interface labels it as measured, our own calculation or assumption.

 

Terrain from orbit. The base of the whole project is the USGS elevation model of Gale Crater at 1 m per pixel (Calef & Parker, 2016). It was built from stereo pairs of HiRISE, the high-resolution camera on NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO), and levelled to HRSC on ESA’s Mars Express and to MOLA, the laser altimeter of Mars Global Surveyor. We resampled it to different scales for each use:

·       2 m for the area around Curiosity’s current position;

·       4 m for the 6.6 × 17.4 km strip of the full traverse;

·       5 m, summarized to 20 m cells, for the 20 km expedition zone.

 

For surface detail we used the USGS HiRISE mosaics of Gale: a 25 cm grayscale orthophoto and a color mosaic, which we used at 3 m. Beyond Gale, the background of the scene combines the global CTX mosaic (MRO, 5 m per pixel, Murray Lab), the MOLA global relief model and the Viking color mosaic (MDIM 2.1). We checked MOLA against our detailed model and found an agreement of +5 ± 41 m.

 

Minerals, sand and thermal data. To explain what an astronaut would find at each stop, we used the CRISM mosaics of Gale (MRO, 19.3 m per pixel) prepared for Curiosity’s landing site selection (Seelos et al., 2012). They map hydrated minerals, clays, sulfates and iron oxides. Sand is a real hazard: Curiosity had to abandon the sandy floor of Hidden Valley in 2014. Since there is no sand map for the whole zone, we used the THEMIS night-time infrared mosaic (Mars Odyssey, 100 m per pixel) as an indicator: loose sand cools faster at night. As a check, Curiosity’s real path never crossed the coldest 10% of the terrain. For regional geology we also used published THEMIS decorrelation-stretch imagery (Anderson & Bell, 2010) and our own color enhancement of Viking and HiRISE images.

 

 

 

Measurements on the ground by Curiosity. Curiosity gives Gale something no other candidate site has: more than 38 km of ground truth since 2012.

·       Traverse: its real path comes from the PDS PLACES localization data and NASA’s mission map (up to sol 5073).

·       49 drill sites: we located each one by matching its drilling sol with NASA’s waypoint records. For each site we gathered:

o   the mineralogy from CheMin;

o   the chemistry from APXS;

o   the evolved gases and organics from SAM, all from the NASA Planetary Data System and the Gale Crater mineralogy database (Bristow & Lafuente);

o   the close-up images from MAHLI.

 

·       RAD: an average surface dose of 0.64 mSv per day (Hassler et al., 2014), about 50% higher near solar minimum (Guo et al., 2021). During the solar storm of 20 May 2024 it recorded 8.1 mGy.

·       REMS:

o   air and ground temperatures (from about +16 °C to −100 °C);

o   pressure, which drops from 848 to 784 Pa as the rover climbs about 1,000 m;

o   ultraviolet radiation, wind and humidity, through sol 4995.

·       DAN: water in the shallow subsurface, between 0 and 6.1% (Mitrofanov et al., 2022).

 

References for astronauts and vehicles. Because no one has walked on Mars, the human limits come from NASA engineering documents, most of them lunar:

·       suit outings of 6 hours nominal and 8 hours maximum (xEMU);

·       slopes up to 20° (Artemis surface requirements);

·       a metabolic cost of about 1,700 BTU/h walking in a suit under Mars gravity (Ogilvie et al., 2026).

 

For the PMR we followed NASA’s Mars Design Reference Architecture 5.0: two crew members, about 3 km/h and a range of around 100 km. We also used the Space Exploration Vehicle concept for suitport exit times under 10 minutes. Radiation limits come from NASA-STD-3001: 600 mSv over a career and 250 mSv per solar event. Shielding values compare a rover cabin (about 1 g/cm²) with a storm shelter (20 g/cm²).

 

What we calculated and what we assumed. From these data we calculated:

·       slope

·       the fraction of sky blocked by the relief

·       the radiation dose along each route, reducing the surface dose by 25% of the blocked sky (calibrated with RAD measurements at Murray Buttes; Ehresmann et al., 2021)

·       safe routes with an A* search

·       walking times with Tobler’s hiking function

·       line of sight between the astronaut and the rover

·       the suitability map that places the habitat away from hazards and from Curiosity’s historic traverse.

 

The 30-minute limit to shelter, the 30-minute reserve and the antenna heights are our own assumptions, marked as provisional in the interface. The 0.64 mSv per day is an average, and the slope and suit limits are borrowed from lunar requirements.

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

Terrain analysis

The terrain analysis turns the elevation model and the orbital images into the answers a crew needs: where the ground is too steep, where it hides sand, where the relief protects from radiation, how far each point is from shelter and where a base could be placed. Each result became a layer of the 3D scene.

 

Slope and hazard classes. We calculated slope cell by cell, correcting east–west distances for latitude. Because a walking astronaut or a moving rover does not feel a single 2 m cell, the tool measures the slope that matters for travel over a 10 m window along each route, and the hazard map uses the mean slope over 6 m to remove isolated spikes. The terrain is classified as caution (15–20°), danger (20–30°) and critical (above 30°). At this resolution Mount Sharp is demanding: much of the ground around Curiosity’s current position is steeper than 20°, which is why routes cannot simply be drawn by eye. Our first hand-drawn routes crossed 54 m (rover) and 110 m (astronaut) of terrain above the limit.

 

Relief, roughness and visibility. Around the boxwork, where Curiosity works today, we produced contour lines every 2 m and 10 m, a hillshade and a topographic position index. The index separates ridges and hollows from the surrounding ground and helps identify the boxwork ridges and the outcrops at each stop. We computed what can be seen from the Altadena drill site and rendered the view from an astronaut’s eye height. The same line-of-sight method, run over the 20 m terrain and including the curvature of Mars, tells whether the astronaut on foot and the rover can see each other. Without that, there is no direct radio contact.

 

Sky blocked by the relief. Hills and cliffs block part of the sky and therefore part of the cosmic radiation. For every cell we measured the horizon angle in 16 directions up to 400 m away and calculated the fraction of sky that is blocked. The scene shows it in four bands: 5–10%, 10–20%, 20–30% and over 30%, each with its dose rate. Along Curiosity’s whole traverse, the most protected point was the Paraitepuy pass, with 32% of the sky blocked. The most protected drill sites were Tapo Caparo (19%), Quela and Hutton (17.5%).

 

 

 

 

Sand. Sand cannot be seen in the elevation model, so we combined three independent indicators:

·       the dark bluish tone of basaltic sand in the HiRISE color mosaic;

·       strong volcanic-mineral signals in CRISM;

·       the coldest ground at night in THEMIS.

 

80% of the sand detected by color coincides with the CRISM signal. The rover avoids the coldest 10% of the THEMIS night image, which Curiosity itself never crossed in 14 years. Possible sand is a danger for the rover and a caution for the astronaut.

 

Routes and reach on foot. Safe routes are calculated with an A* search over the terrain, with separate rules for the rover and the astronaut and a preference for shaded ground on foot. None of the calculated routes has a segment above 20°. Near Curiosity’s current position, the walking route to the farthest stop and back is 2.6 km, takes 84 minutes and adds 36 µSv. To know how far each point is from shelter, we ran a fastest-path search from the base over a 4 m grid, using Tobler’s walking speed and making slopes over 20° four times more costly. The result is a map of minutes back to the base, with contours at 10, 20 and 30 minutes. It showed that some scientific stops lie beyond a 30-minute walk, which is why the expedition carries its shelter with it in the PMR. For the 20 km expedition zone, the rover rule was calibrated on Curiosity’s real path: 99% of the cells it crossed pass the rule.

 

Minerals at each stop. For each stop we sampled the CRISM products in a 3 × 3 pixel window. Fixed thresholds translate them into plain language: sulfates, hydrated minerals, clays, hematite, volcanic sand or no clear signal. With the same data we chose five new stops south of Curiosity’s current position. Each one follows a different criterion: strongest hydrated sulfate, highest viewpoint, most sheltered spot, strongest clay signal and the southernmost reachable flat ground.

 

Where to place the habitat. Finally, we built a suitability map to choose the landing and habitat site. We first excluded:

·       landing slopes over 10° (measured over 20 m)

·       rough terrain

·       sand plus 250 m

·       anything within 150 m of a rover hazard

·       anything within 1 km of Curiosity’s traverse or drill sites, and within 2 km of its 2012 landing site and current position, to preserve them as heritage.

The remaining ground was scored by flatness, distance to hazards, closeness to the traverse, roughness and low elevation. Only 9% of the strip qualifies, all of it on the plains west of the 2012 landing site. We chose zone 2 (4.617° S, 137.375° E, −4,487 m): it has a 2.4° slope, lies 1.7 km from the traverse and 1.1 km from the nearest hazard, and offers a fully suitable circle 439 m in radius for the lander and the base. The landing site proposed for Gale in 2015 (Calef et al.) falls inside our exclusion zones: it lies 757 m from the traverse and 1.3 km from Curiosity’s landing site.

 

Seeing the terrain. To highlight geological units that look alike in normal color, we applied a decorrelation stretch to Viking and HiRISE images. We also rendered an oblique 3D view of the whole traverse on the HiRISE color mosaic, which we used as the general picture of the mission.

 

 

 

 

 

 

Limitations & next steps

Gale Crater is the best-measured place on Mars, so the terrain itself is real data: elevation, imagery and minerals come directly from NASA and USGS products. Our main limitations lie elsewhere. The most important is that no one has ever walked on Mars in a suit, so the human limits we use are borrowed from the Moon and from Earth. The 20° slope limit comes from NASA’s lunar surface requirements, walking speed follows a terrestrial hiking model, and the 30-minute shelter rule is our own assumption based on solar storm warning times. Radiation is also an average: the 0.64 mSv per day measured by Curiosity’s RAD instrument covers only one part of the solar cycle, and the real dose changes with solar activity and season. Our terrain-shielding factor was calibrated at a single location.

 

The data also have limits of scale. Our elevation model, at 2 to 4 m per pixel, cannot show rocks smaller than that, and it was precisely small, sharp rocks on these plains that damaged Curiosity’s wheels. Part of the expedition is conceptual: the Pressurized Mars Rover, the deep drilling and the deployed instruments do not yet exist for Mars and are simulated in the tool. Finally, four of the 49 drill-site cards still rely on raw data and have not yet been checked against a published source; they are marked as such.

 

Our first step is to apply the same method beyond Gale. Jezero Crater is a natural next site, because Perseverance provides the same kind of ground truth that Curiosity gives us here. The ice-rich mid-latitude regions, such as Arcadia and Amazonis Planitia, are today’s leading candidates for crewed landings.

 

We also want to make the astronaut tools richer:

·       Communication: using our line-of-sight analysis, the tool could show at every point of a route whether the astronaut on foot can see, and therefore communicate with, the crew member in the rover.

·       Radiation: dose would follow the solar cycle and respond to real space-weather alerts instead of a fixed average.

·       Suit power: the outing budget would include the extra power needed to stay warm in cold, shaded terrain.

 

Finally, these limits should be validated outside the screen, through tests at Mars analog stations on Earth such as the Mars Desert Research Station, and with data from real suit trials. That way the borrowed numbers can be replaced with measured ones.

 

Tools & AI use

Geospatial processing. We processed the orbital data with open-source remote sensing and GIS tools. We used SNAP (ESA’s Sentinel Application Platform) to read, combine and inspect the rasters. QGIS, with GDAL from the OSGeo4W distribution, handled cropping, reprojection and terrain analysis. All layers share the same coordinate system used by NASA’s Curiosity products: an equirectangular projection on a Mars sphere of radius 3,396,190 m. That lets every dataset line up with the rover’s real traverse.

 

Data sources. The base of the project is the USGS elevation model of Gale Crater at 1 m per pixel. It was built from HiRISE stereo images (Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter) and levelled to HRSC (ESA’s Mars Express) and MOLA (Mars Global Surveyor). On top of it we used HiRISE color and 25 cm imagery for surface detail, and CRISM (MRO) mosaics for the minerals at each stop. For regional context we used THEMIS (Mars Odyssey) and Viking orbiter imagery. From the ground, Curiosity contributed:

·       its real traverse and 49 drill sites (PDS PLACES);

·       surface radiation from RAD;

·       weather from REMS;

·       subsurface water from DAN;

·       the mineralogy of its drill samples from CheMin and SAM.

 

We also reviewed other orbital datasets (OMEGA, TES, GRS, SHARAD, MARSIS, CaSSIS, FREND and the Emirates Mars Mission) to understand the context of Gale, but they are not part of the final map.

 

Terrain analysis. From the elevation model we derived:

·       slope, hillshade, contour lines and terrain roughness (topographic position index);

·       line-of-sight maps from the astronaut’s point of view;

·       the fraction of sky blocked by the relief, which lowers the radiation dose.

·       We enhanced subtle color differences with a decorrelation stretch on Viking and HiRISE imagery. We built a suitability analysis to place the habitat away from hazards and from Curiosity’s historic traverse. Routes are computed with an A* search that respects separate slope limits for the rover and the astronaut.

 

 

 

 

3D experience. The interactive scene is written in JavaScript with three.js (MIT license) and runs in a browser, offline, from a single file. A Python script (NumPy, SciPy, Pillow) packages the terrain, imagery, routes and parameters into that page. We also tested NASA’s open-source MMGIS map server (Apache 2.0). The rover, PMR and astronaut models, the routes and every number shown on screen are generated from the data above.

 

Use of AI. We used Claude (Anthropic), through Claude Code, as a development and research assistant:

·       writing and debugging the processing scripts and the 3D scene;

·       searching for and summarizing scientific sources;

·       checking calculations;

·       drafting and translating documentation.

 

Every value used in the tool was checked against its original source. Each one is labelled as measured, our own calculation or assumption, and assumptions are marked as provisional in the interface. Design decisions, the choice of site and stops, and the final review were made by the team.

 

 

Software utilization

Exploration and navigation

  • 3D globe of Mars with MOLA + HRSC relief, and 25 cm imagery on 1 m terrain inside Gale crater
  • Search for drill sites, zones, base sites, orbiters, Mars landmarks and coordinates
  • Map controls: compass, 2D/3D, relief exaggeration ×1–×3, live coordinates, elevation and scale
  • Real night sky (Hipparcos stars and the Milky Way)
  • Mobile use: open the app on a phone on the same Wi-Fi by scanning a QR code

 

Routes and traverses

  • Rover route (A) with slope and sand limits, wheel tracks and dust
  • Walking route (B) with the suit slope limit, walking time and radiation dose
  • Crewed rover route (PMR) from the base: A* path (slope ≤ 20°, avoids sand) with battery energy along the way
  • South expedition (E1–E5), by rover or on foot
  • Curiosity’s real traverse from 2012 to today, replayed sol by sol and stopping at every drill site
  • Guided tour of the stops, each with its scientific reason
  • Free drive and free walk (WASD or joystick) with live warnings

 

Pins and destinations

  • Destination pin on the terrain: computes the rover and astronaut routes there and back, with distance, time, dose and slope
  • Pin system for the 49 drill sites and for our routes and stops, with on/off toggles
  • Pins colored by resource (water, CO₂, iron, chlorine, mineral)

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

Samples (drill sites)

  • 49 drill-site records:
    • MAHLI photo
    • Minerals (CheMin), chemistry (APXS) and gases (SAM), each with its verification status
    • Water available for a base (team calculation)
    • Links to the raw data
  • Side-by-side table to compare drill sites
  • Simulated 2 m drilling by the crewed rover, labeled as a simulation

 

Crew mission simulation

  • Two-astronaut mission:
    • Astronaut 1’s helmet camera view
    • Astronaut 2’s HUD with ground type, CRISM minerals, radiation, nearest shelter, next stop and a minimap
  • Communications: the Mars base answers instantly; Earth control answers after the real light-time delay
  • Helmet HUD while walking and the PMR rover screen
  • Mission timer showing time outside (T+hh:mm)

 

Safety and hazard analysis

  • Slope hazard layer: caution 15–20°, danger 20–30°, critical over 30°
  • Possible loose sand layer from HiRISE color, labeled as an indicator
  • Radiation dose (RAD, 0.64 mSv/day) with its day/night variation
  • Terrain shielding (the fraction of sky the relief blocks)
  • Live alerts in 4 levels: info, caution, danger, critical
  • Walk limits: 6 h nominal, 8 h maximum, 30 min from shelter, 30 min reserve

 

Science layers

  • CRISM mineral layers (clays, sulfates, mafic, hydrated and others)
  • Whole-Mars layers: MOLA altitude colors, THEMIS night infrared, IAU place names, landing sites, current day/night
  • Climate by date: solar longitude (Ls), Martian season, REMS data
  • Live clock: UTC, Mars year, Ls and season in Gale (Mars24 algorithm)

 

 

 

Base planning

  • Three candidate base sites compared by nearby water and carbonates, measured slope and atmosphere
    • Curiosity
    • GX-2 rover with wings, drone and drill
    • PMR pressurized rover with wings, crab mode, drone, drill and suitports

 

Orbiters and context

  • Orbits of MRO, Mars Odyssey, Mars Express, ExoMars TGO and Hope (from JPL Horizons), each with its mission and its next pass over Gale
  • Phobos and Deimos
  • Timeline from the formation of Gale and the first telescopes to every mission that reached Mars or tried to

 

Knowledge base (wiki)

  • Searchable wiki: why Gale, stops, drill sites, south expedition, climate, rover vs. astronaut, communications, Gale Base, vehicles and sources
  • Any record opens in its own tab, without the globe
  • Every data point has its source behind a “?” circle
  • Measured, calculated and assumed values are kept apart, with the labels “provisional”, “to verify” and “SIMULATION”

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

Discarded ideas

Many ideas changed or were dropped during the 48 hours. We keep them here because each one taught us something about the data or about the problem.

 

Ideas we tried and corrected

 

Routes drawn by eye. Our first routes from Curiosity’s current position were drawn by hand over the image. When we measured them on the real terrain, they crossed 54 m (rover) and 110 m (astronaut) of slopes above 20°. We replaced them with calculated routes, and kept the hand-drawn ones in the scene, semi-transparent, as a reminder of why a planner is needed.

 

Filling the gaps with lower-quality terrain. To show a wider area, we first extended the high-resolution color terrain with a gray, lower-resolution fill. We removed it: it looked like data but was not. Where there is no detailed elevation model, the tool now shows context only and does not calculate routes.

 

A radiation value copied wrong. For a day we used 0.67 mSv per day for the surface dose. Checking the original paper showed the measured value is 0.64 mSv per day (Hassler et al., 2014), and we corrected it in every layer.

 

Sand from CRISM alone. Our first sand layer used CRISM pixels of 19 m. It marked 36% of one route as sandy, often in large blocks. Detecting sand by its tone in the 3 m HiRISE color mosaic, and checking it against CRISM, lowered that to 22% and drew the sand where it really is.

 

Alerts that stopped the astronaut. Early versions blocked movement or showed warnings almost constantly. Walking a full route triggered dozens of messages. We changed them to one alert at a time, with a short delay, so the astronaut is warned but never stopped. A real crew decides; the map advises.

 

Ideas we discarded because of the data

 

“Gale is the best place to land.” We first planned to present Gale as an ideal landing site, following a 2015 NASA workshop proposal (Calef et al.). Current research favors mid-latitude sites with shallow ice, and Gale has almost none. We changed the argument: Gale is the best place to design and validate the tool, because it has the most ground truth. The landing site proposed in 2015 also turned out to lie 757 m from Curiosity’s traverse, so our suitability analysis moved the habitat to a new zone.

 

The rover as a storm shelter. We wanted the PMR to protect the crew during a solar storm. NASA studies give a rover cabin about 1 g/cm² of shielding, while a storm shelter needs around 20 g/cm². Inside the PMR, the tool counts the same dose as outside.

 

A faster rover. We started with 10 km/h for the PMR, from NASA’s lunar Space Exploration Vehicle. For Mars, NASA’s Design Reference Architecture 5.0 uses about 3 km/h, so that became the default.

 

Collecting samples from Curiosity. We imagined the crew retrieving samples from the rover. Curiosity does not store samples: each one is analyzed inside the rover. The expedition now ends next to Curiosity, where the astronauts collect their own.

 

Ideas we set aside for later

There was not enough time to build some ideas, even though the data for several of them are already prepared:

·       Communication windows: mark when MRO, Mars Odyssey or TGO pass overhead to relay data. Their orbits are already calculated in the tool.

·       Solar power by hour and season: power for the PMR or a solar base from the Sun’s angle and the dust measured by REMS.

·       Dust storm forecasts: use Mars Climate Sounder data or MARCI’s daily images.

·       A resource map for a base: water that is easy to extract, perchlorates and nitrates as a colored layer over Gale. A related idea is a real water estimate from clays and amorphous material, with its uncertainty range.

·       Showing uncertainty: ranges for dose and time instead of a single number.

·       Terrain classification from photos: use Curiosity’s 1,315 images to recognize rocks, sand and veins automatically.

·       Jezero and Perseverance: run the same tool on a second ground-truthed site. The terrain is already prepared.

·       Shared planning: several people at once, with roles for the base, the astronaut and Earth.

·       Other formats: export routes to NASA’s MMGIS, which we already tested, and versions for virtual or augmented reality headsets.
